title: Automatic Generation and Evaluation of Reading Comprehension Test Items with Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating and evaluating multiple-choice reading comprehension items. The authors argue that manual item development is time-consuming and that common automatic metrics for generated questions are poorly suited to reading comprehension tasks, so they propose a new evaluation approach based on answerability and guessability.

The intervention studied is the use of large language models, specifically Llama 2 Chat and GPT-4, to generate German reading comprehension items in a zero-shot setting and to evaluate those items by answering them with and without the source text. The paper introduces a new metric, text informativity, defined as the difference between answerability and guessability. It also compares human judgment with LLM-based evaluation and reports item quality ratings and inter-annotator agreement.

The dataset came from German online language courses offered by Deutsche Welle, targeting non-native speakers at about CEFR B1 level. Human annotators were six native German-speaking university students or recent graduates who judged items from ten texts, while automatic evaluation was run on fifty texts. The authors find that GPT-4-generated items generally outperform Llama 2 items and are closest to human-written items in text informativity and quality ratings. GPT-4 is also the most human-like evaluator, while Llama 2 is less reliable. The paper concludes that zero-shot LLMs are promising for reading-comprehension item generation and that text informativity is a useful evaluation metric, though it does not capture all aspects of item quality.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A large language model/chat model family used for zero-shot text generation and response evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of two instruction-tuned LLMs to generate multiple-choice reading comprehension items from German texts and to automatically evaluate item answerability/guessability with and without the text.

findings.finding_summary: On zero-shot generation, LLaMA 2 produced acceptable-quality items but clearly underperformed GPT-4 on text informativity and human quality ratings. For text informativity, LLaMA 2 generated items scored 0.160 with human evaluators and 0.129 with GPT-4 as evaluator; these were the lowest among the generators. Human raters also gave LLaMA 2 the lowest average quality, including 11/180 unusable ratings.
findings.measure: Text informativity; human quality ratings; response accuracy with/without text
findings.confidence_interval: [0.109, 0.213] (human evaluator text informativity); [0.082, 0.178] (GPT-4 evaluator text informativity)
findings.sample_size: generation test set n=50 texts; human evaluation subset n=10 texts

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a small human-evaluation subset and no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison in an educational intervention sense. It is methodologically careful for item-generation/evaluation, but evidence for K-12 instruction outcomes is indirect.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects concern item quality and evaluability rather than learner achievement. The only numeric differences are modest-to-medium in the item-quality domain, but they do not translate to direct reading gains.
